title: Escrow account and analysis definitions
content: An escrow account is controlled by a servicer to pay property-related charges such as taxes and insurance on a federally related mortgage loan. An escrow analysis is a trial running balance used to set target balances and future deposits and to determine whether a shortage, surplus, or deficiency exists.

title: Shortage, surplus, deficiency, and target balance
content: A shortage is the amount by which the current escrow balance is below its target at analysis. A surplus is the amount above target, while a deficiency is a negative balance. The target balance is the estimated month-end amount just sufficient for remaining disbursements, scheduled deposits, and any permitted cushion.

title: Escrow items paid in installments
content: An escrow item is a category of expenditure such as property tax or insurance. Multiple installments to the same tax authority remain one escrow item even when the jurisdiction bills and receives payment more than once during the computation year.

title: Initial escrow deposit limit
content: When an escrow account is created, the servicer may collect enough for charges attributable to the period before the first payment. The projected lowest month-end target is calculated at zero, after which a cushion of no more than one-sixth of estimated annual escrow payments may be added.

title: Monthly escrow payment and cushion limits
content: During the life of an escrow account, the regular monthly escrow charge may equal one-twelfth of reasonably anticipated annual disbursements. A servicer may also maintain a cushion, but the cushion cannot exceed one-sixth of estimated annual disbursements.

title: Analysis before creating an escrow account
content: A servicer must analyze the escrow account before establishment to determine both the initial deposit and periodic payment. Estimates must follow the regulation's disbursement rules, use dates that avoid penalties, and support an initial statement and any required shortage, surplus, or deficiency adjustment.

title: Annual escrow analysis requirement
content: At the end of each escrow computation year, the servicer must perform another analysis to determine payments for the next year. It must estimate upcoming disbursements, determine any shortage, surplus, or deficiency, make the permitted adjustment, and provide an annual escrow statement.

title: Aggregate accounting and maximum cushion
content: Escrow analyses must use aggregate accounting, evaluating the account as a whole rather than separately padding each item. The cushion is optional and may be lower or zero, but it may never exceed one-sixth of estimated annual disbursements.

title: Estimating future escrow disbursements
content: If the next year's charge is known, the servicer must use that amount. If it is unknown, the estimate may generally use the preceding year's charge or that charge adjusted by no more than the most recent annual change in the CPI for all urban consumers; comparable property may be used for unassessed new construction.

title: Loan documents can impose a lower cushion
content: The servicer must examine the mortgage documents for the applicable escrow cushion. A contractual lower limit controls, while contract language allowing a larger amount cannot override Regulation X's maximum. Other federal or state law may also impose a lower limit.

title: Aggregate trial running balance
content: Aggregate analysis projects scheduled escrow deposits and disbursements across the computation year to find the account's low point and maximum permitted target balances. These procedures establish ceilings; a servicer may use a smaller cushion or accounting method that produces lower balances.

title: Escrow statements after servicing transfer
content: If a transferee changes the monthly payment or accounting method, it must provide an initial escrow statement within 60 days after transfer. If it retains both, it may continue the transferor's computation year or establish another year through a short-year statement, followed by an analysis and annual statement.

title: Transferred shortages and surpluses
content: A new servicer must treat shortages, surpluses, and deficiencies already present in a transferred escrow account under the same procedures that govern other escrow analyses. A transfer does not create a separate rule allowing those balances to be discarded or reset.

title: Handling escrow surpluses
content: For a borrower who is current at analysis, a surplus of at least $50 must be refunded within 30 days. A smaller surplus may be refunded or credited against next year's payments. Different treatment may apply when payments are more than 30 days overdue.

title: Shortage below one monthly escrow payment
content: When a shortage is less than one monthly escrow payment, the servicer may leave it in place, require repayment within 30 days, or spread repayment through equal monthly payments over a period of at least 12 months.

title: Shortage of at least one monthly escrow payment
content: When a shortage equals or exceeds one monthly escrow payment, the servicer may leave it in place or collect it through equal monthly payments over at least 12 months. The rule does not authorize demanding this larger shortage in a single 30-day payment.

title: Annual notice of shortage or deficiency
content: The servicer must notify the borrower at least once during the computation year when the account has a shortage or deficiency. The notification may appear in the annual escrow statement or in a separate notice.

title: Initial escrow statement timing and contents
content: For an escrow account required as a loan condition, the initial statement is due at settlement or within 45 calendar days. It identifies the mortgage and escrow portions of the monthly payment, estimated item amounts and payment dates, the selected cushion, and the trial running balance.

title: Annual escrow statement history and projection
content: Within 30 days after each computation year, the annual statement must report account history and next-year projections. Required items include prior and current payment components, total deposits and disbursements, ending balance, and explanations for handling any surplus, shortage, or deficiency.

title: Transferor short-year statement
content: After servicing transfers, the transferor must provide a short-year annual escrow statement within 60 days of the transfer's effective date. The short-year statement closes the prior computation period and supports continuity into the transferee's records.

title: Timely escrow disbursements and advances
content: When the borrower is not more than 30 days overdue, the servicer must pay escrow items on or before the deadline needed to avoid a penalty. If the account lacks funds, the servicer must advance them and may recover the resulting deficiency under the shortage and deficiency rules.

title: Property-tax installment payments
content: When a taxing authority offers both annual and installment payment and provides no annual discount or installment surcharge, the servicer must pay property taxes in installments. This rule affects expected dates and helps distinguish legitimate installments from accidental duplicate disbursements.

title: Notice required for servicing transfers
content: Unless a stated exclusion applies, both the transferor and transferee must notify the borrower when mortgage servicing is assigned, sold, or transferred. The notice must contain the required transfer information, and the parties may use the model form in Appendix MS-2.

title: Transfers excluded from notice rules
content: Certain affiliate, merger or acquisition, and master-servicer transfers are excluded when the payee, payment address, account number, and payment amount do not change. An assignment of an FHA-insured mortgage to FHA is also excluded from FHA's notice obligation.

title: Ordinary servicing-transfer notice timing
content: Normally, the transferor gives notice at least 15 days before the effective date and the transferee gives notice no later than 15 days after it. A combined notice is permitted when delivered at least 15 days before the transfer becomes effective.

title: Extended and settlement notice timing
content: A notice may be delivered up to 30 days after transfer when specified events such as termination for cause, servicer bankruptcy, or an FDIC or NCUA proceeding precede the transfer. Separate or combined notices supplied at settlement satisfy the ordinary timing rule.

title: Transfer notice dates and contact information
content: A transfer notice identifies the effective date and contact information for both the old and new servicers. It also states when the transferor stops and the transferee begins accepting payments; those two dates must be identical or consecutive.

title: Insurance and loan terms in transfer notice
content: The notice explains whether optional insurance is affected and what the borrower must do to maintain it. It must also state that transferring servicing does not change loan terms or conditions except for terms directly related to servicing.

title: Sixty-day protection for misdirected payments
content: For 60 days beginning on the transfer's effective date, an on-time payment sent to the old servicer cannot be treated as late. The protection includes the contractual grace period and prohibits imposing a late fee merely because the payment went to the transferor.

title: Transferor handling of misdirected payments
content: Starting on the effective transfer date, the old servicer must promptly address payments it receives by mistake. It must either forward the payment to the new servicer for application to the loan or return it to the sender with notice identifying the correct recipient.

title: Reasonably designed servicing policies and procedures
content: A servicer must maintain policies and actual practices reasonably designed to achieve the regulation's servicing objectives. The specific design may reflect the operation's size, scope, portfolio, credit risk, and complaint history, but flexibility does not remove the required objectives.

title: Accurate information and complaint correction
content: Policies and procedures must support accurate, timely borrower disclosures and the investigation, response, and appropriate correction of borrower complaints. They must also allow prompt retrieval of information from service providers when provider actions caused an error.

title: Oversight of servicing providers
content: Servicer personnel need access to current documents reflecting provider actions and enough information to periodically review provider compliance. Policies must also facilitate accurate status sharing among servicing, loss-mitigation, and foreclosure personnel where applicable.

title: Transferor duty to transfer accurate information
content: A transferor's policies must timely deliver every controlled document and item of information related to the transferred loan. The form and manner must preserve accuracy and allow the transferee to satisfy obligations to the loan owner and applicable law.

title: Electronic boarding and document identification
content: Electronic transfer is permitted when procedures protect accuracy and legal compliance. Transferor systems should support prompt, correct boarding into the transferee's platform and ensure that all necessary documents and information are available and identifiable after transfer.

title: Loss-mitigation information in transfer
content: Transfer procedures should include the current status of borrower loss-mitigation discussions, agreements already reached, and relevant recovery analysis for non-performing loans. These records are part of the information that must remain usable across the servicing transfer.

title: Transferee obtains missing documents from transferor
content: A transferee must identify necessary information that did not arrive and obtain it from the transferor. For loss-mitigation records, procedures should seek missing agreements and related documents from the prior servicer before asking the borrower to resubmit them.

title: Servicing-file transaction history
content: The servicing file includes a schedule of every credit and debit to the mortgage account, including escrow and suspense-account transactions. It also includes core loan instruments, servicing communication notes, and applicable system data fields, subject to the regulation's request procedures and limits.

section: A. General Transfer-Related Policies and Procedures
title: Pre-transfer contracts, instructions, and system testing
content: CFPB guidance identifies useful pre-transfer controls: contracts requiring necessary records at boarding, deal-specific instructions, early coordination about data fields and indexing, compatibility and mapping tests, and quality control comparing preliminary data in the transferee system with transferor submissions.

section: A. General Transfer-Related Policies and Procedures
title: Staging transfers that cannot board safely at once
content: When a transfer cannot be completed reliably in one batch, the guidance describes using alternative protocols such as multiple smaller transactions. The goal is to preserve the transferee's ability to meet servicing obligations for every transferred loan rather than forcing a technically unsafe cutover.

section: A. General Transfer-Related Policies and Procedures
title: Post-transfer validation and issue resolution
content: Post-transfer controls include validating that inbound data transferred correctly and remains functional, identifying and correcting data errors, organizing incoming records, using transferred information before contacting borrowers, and maintaining regular transferor calls to resolve loan-level issues quickly.

section: A. General Transfer-Related Policies and Procedures
title: Flagging pending loss-mitigation loans
content: For loans in loss mitigation, the transferor should clearly flag complete and incomplete applications and approved plans, including trial modifications. The transferee should receive detailed loan lists and supporting documentation early enough for its systems and personnel to continue processing.

section: A. General Transfer-Related Policies and Procedures
title: Use transferred documents before burdening borrowers
content: The guidance expects a transferee to review and use transferred loss-mitigation materials. Routinely requiring borrowers to resubmit documents, failing to identify what is still needed, or failing to evaluate transferred applications may indicate that policies are not reasonably designed under section 1024.38.

section: A. General Transfer-Related Policies and Procedures
title: Scrutiny of information sent after boarding
content: CFPB examiners may scrutinize a practice of waiting until after boarding to send information already held before boarding. Subject to genuine legal limits on pre-sale sharing, transferors should make every effort to provide information before boarding so both servicers can meet transfer and evaluation obligations.

section: B. Applicability of Other Parts of the New Servicing Rule
title: Error notices and information requests survive transfer
content: A transferee must answer applicable borrower error notices and information requests on time even when the underlying event occurred under the transferor. A transferor also retains certain response obligations after transfer, and transferring a loan soon after receiving a request does not cancel the response deadline.

section: C. Protections under Federal Consumer Financial Law
title: Compliance management and consumer remediation
content: The guidance expects a robust compliance management system that prevents, detects, and remediates violations during transfers. When a problem is found, corrective action should both prevent recurrence on later transfers and address actual harm to affected borrowers promptly and at an appropriate scope.

section: D. Plans for Handling Servicing Transfers
title: Information in a significant-transfer plan
content: For significant transfers, CFPB may request a written risk-management plan covering loan count and balance, platform compatibility, legal compliance, transaction and system testing, error correction timeframes, staff training, and customer service for loss-mitigation requests and pending applications.
